Lakṣmī
------------------------------------------
For obvious reasons, लक्ष्मी, the goddess of fortune, is more sought after than सरस्वती, the goddess of learning. Being the power and consort of विष्णु, the preserver, she is represented as the power of multiplicity and the goddess of fortune, both of which are equally necessary in the process of preservation.
‘Śrī’ or ‘Lakṣmī’, as depicted in the Veda, is the goddess of wealth and fortune, power and beauty. Though there is scope for the supposition that Śrī and लक्ष्मी are two separate deities, the descriptions of them are so identical, that we are tempted to conclude that they represent one and the same deity. Some scholars opine that ‘Śrī’ was a pre-vedic deity connected with fertility, water and agriculture. She was later fused with लक्ष्मी, the Vedic goddess of beauty.
In her first इन्चर्नतिओन्, according to the पुराणस्, she was the daughter of the sage भृगु and his wife ख्याति. She was later born out of the ocean of milk at the time of its churning. She, being the consort of विष्णु, is born as his spouse whenever he incarnates. When he appeared as वामन, परशुराम, राम and कृष्ण, she appeared as Padmā (or Kamalā), Dharaṇī, सीता and रुक्मिणी. She is as inseparable from विष्णु as speech from meaning or knowledge from intellect, or good deeds from righteousness. He represents all that is masculine, and she, all that is feminine.
Lakṣmī is usually described as enchantingly beautiful and standing on a lotus, and holding lotuses in each of her two hands. It is because of this, perhaps, that she is named as Padmā or Kamalā. She is also adorned with a lotus garland. Very often elephants are shown on either side, emptying pitchers of water over her, the pitchers being presented by celestial maidens. Her colour is variously described as dark, pink, golden yellow or white. While in the company of विष्णु, she is shown with two hands only. When worshipped in a temple—separate temples for लक्ष्मी are rather rare—she is shown seated on a lotus throne, with four hands holding पद्म, शङ्ख, अमृतकलश (pot of ambrosia) and बिल्व fruit. Sometimes, another kind of fruit, the Mātuliṅga (a citron) is shown instead of बिल्व. When shown with eight hands, bow and arrow, mace and discus are added. This is actually the महालक्ष्मी, an aspect of दुर्गा.
We can now attempt an explanation that is behind this highly symbolical picture. If लक्ष्मी is pictured as dark in complexion, it is to show that she is the consort of विष्णु, the dark god. If golden yellow, that shows her as the source of all wealth. If white, she represents the purest form of प्रकृति (nature) from which the universe has developed. The pinkish complexion, which is more common, reflects her compassion for creatures, since she is the मोथेर् of all.
Her four hands signify her power to grant the four पुरुषार्थस् (ends of human life), धर्म (righteousness), अर्थ (wealth), काम (pleasures of the flesh) and मोक्ष (beatitude).
The lotuses, in various stages of blooming, represent the worlds and beings in various stages of evolution.
The fruit stands for the fruits of our labours. However-much we may toil and labour, unless the मोथेर् is gracious enough to grant the fruits of our labour, nothing will be of any avail. If the fruit is a coconut—with its shell, kernel and water—it means that from her originate the three levels of च्रेअतिओन्, the gross, the subtle and the extremely subtle. If it is a pomegranate or a citron, it signifies that the various created worlds are under her control and that she transcends them all. If it is a बिल्व fruit—which, incidentally, is not very tasty or attractive, but which is extremely good for health—it stands for मोक्ष, the highest fruit of spiritual life.
Amṛtakalaśa also signifies the same thing, viz., that she can give us the bliss of इम्मोर्तलित्य्.
In some of the sculptural depictions of लक्ष्मी, the owl is shown as her carrier-vehicle. It looks rather odd and strange that the goddess of fortune and beauty should have an ugly bird, the very sight of which is considered inauspicious, as her carrier! Once the symbolical significance of this oddity is unravelled, we will be in a better position to appreciate the poor bird and its compassionate mistress!
The word in Sanskrit for the owl is Ulūka. Ulūka is also one of the names of इन्द्र, the king of gods! Hence लक्ष्मी being the goddess of fortune could not have found a better person to ride on, than the king of gods, who personifies all the wealth, power and glory that a living being can aspire for in life. At the same time, here is a warning administered to the seekers of secular wealth, instead of spiritual wealth, by comparing even the glory of इन्द्र to the ugliness of an inelegant and partially blind bird.
Based on the beautiful description given in the Bhagavadgītā (2.69) we can be generous enough to compare our owl to the स्थितप्रज्ञ, the man of steady wisdom. Then, the symbol would mean that मोथेर् लक्ष्मी is the mistress of spiritual wisdom. If we are not so generous, then, we can learn a lesson from it in another way, viz., ‘Do not shut out your eyes to the light of wisdom coming from the sun of knowledge!’ Out of consideration for mankind, the all-compassionate मोथेर् has kept this personification of इग्नोरन्चे under her control.

lakṣaṇā
(‘implication’)
------------------------------------------
There are three ways in which words can express their meanings. The direct way or vācya is the first, as for instance in ‘ayaḥ,’ which means iron. The meaning hinted at or vyaṅgya is the second, as in ‘saśaṅkhacakro hariḥ,’ ‘Viṣṇu with शङ्ख (conch) and चक्र (discus)’. Here though the word ‘hariḥ’ has several meanings like lion, monkey, यम, वायु or विष्णु, the additional word ‘saśaṅkhacakraḥ’ limits it to विष्णु alone. The implied meaning or lakṣya is the third. For instance in the sentence ‘Kaliṅgaḥ sāhasikaḥ’, ‘The कलिङ्ग is a bold man’, though the word ‘Kaliṅga’ means the country of that name, it means by implication, a citizen of that country.
Implication, called ‘lakṣaṇā’, is of three types: जहल्-लक्षणा, अजहल्-लक्षणा and जहद्-अजहल्-लक्षणा.
In ‘jahal-लक्षणा’, the direct meaning is completely given up (jahad = giving up) in favour of the implied meaning. For example, consider the sentence ‘gaṅgāyāṁ ghoṣaḥ’, ‘The village of cowherds is in the गङ्गा river’. Since a village cannot exist inside a river it is to be interpreted as ‘on the bank of the गङ्गा river’, so near that it looks as if it is under the river.
In ‘ajahal-लक्षणा’ the direct meaning is not altogether given up (ajahad = not giving up) though it cannot also be accepted in toto. For instance, in the sentence ‘śoṇaḥ dhāvati’ (‘red colour is running’), obviously it means a red animal like a horse which is running and not red colour (śoṇa = red) itself.
In ‘jahad-अजहल्-लक्षणा’, a part of the direct meaning is given up and another part is retained. In a sentence like ‘soyaṁ devadattaḥ’ (‘This is that Devadatta’), Devadatta who is seen here and now is recognised as the same person seen earlier in some other place. In this recognition, Devadatta, the person, is retained whereas the time and place are ignored.
It is this ‘jahad-अजहल्-लक्षणा’ that is adopted by the Advaitins while interpreting the famous Vedāntic dicta like tat tvam asi (‘That thou art’) or ahaṁ brahmāsmi (‘I am ब्रह्मन्’).

Lakshmi Venkateswara Steam Press
------------------------------------------
During the period A. D. 1750 to 1900, a lot of interest had been roused among the European scholars and others to know about the ancient and medieval Hindu scriptures. One of the pioneering publishing houses that arose during this time was the लक्स्ह्मि वेन्कतेस्wअर स्तेअम् प्रेस्स्.
It was established in A. D. 1871 in Bombay (now Mumbai) with the sole aim of publishing all the extant Sanskrit and Hindi works of outstanding merit on different subjects. So far, this publishing होउसे has printed as many as 2800 titles. Many of these have been reprinted several times. The subjects covered are philosophy, Indian म्य्थोलोग्य्, the two great epics— Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata—Bhagavad-gītā, classical Sanskrit literature, Astro-logy, आयुर्वेद, मुसिच् and so on.
Its present name and address are: Shri Venkateshwar Press, Mumbai; Khemraj Shrikrishnadas, 91/109, Khemraj Shrikrishnadas Marg, 7th Khetwadi Back Road Corner, Mumbai 400 004, India.
It has branches at Pune, Thane (in Maharashtra) and Vārāṇasi (in Uttar Pradesh).

Lakulīśa
------------------------------------------
The पाशुपत Cult is a prominent aspect of शैविस्म्. (See ŚAIVISM.) It is said to have been started by लकुलीश (or नकुलीश), supposed to be the 28th (and the last) human इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord शिव. Since he used to hold a lakula (or club) always, he came to be known as लकुलीश.
The village Karjaṇ near Baroda in Gujarat seems to have been the place where he lived.
He had four disciples: Kuśika, मित्र, गर्ग and Kauruṣya.
The town Jharpatan in Gujarat has a temple dedicated to him.
Since the पाशुपत Cult had spread in some parts of Gujarat and South India even by the 6th century A. D. लकुलीश must have lived much earlier.

Lakṣmaṇa
------------------------------------------
As regards the well-known hero लक्ष्मण of the Rāmāyaṇa, see RĀMĀYAṆA for details.
Lakṣmaṇa is also the name of दुर्योधन’s son, considered as a hero. He fought with अभिमन्यु several times and was ultimately killed by him on the 13th day of the कुरुक्षेत्र war.
